costGuide.title: Toyota 1ND-TV Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a 1ND-TV typically takes 6-8 hours at £65/hr (independent specialist rate) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: The replacement cost for a Toyota 1ND-TV engine is heavily influenced by the condition of the turbocharger and fuel injectors. Units with a recently serviced turbo actuator and replaced injector seals command a premium. Always verify if the EGR valve has been cleaned, as carbon buildup is a known wear item on higher-mileage examples. For a full breakdown of what is included in a professional rebuild, see our full reconditioned engine cost guide .

failures.title: Toyota 1ND-TV Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Turbocharger Actuator Wear - 2004-2015 models
items.whatHappens: The variable geometry turbocharger (VGT) on the 1ND-TV is prone to actuator arm wear and sticking vanes due to carbon buildup. This presents as a loss of power, excessive black smoke under acceleration, and the illumination of the check engine light.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacing or repairing the turbo actuator is a standard fix (£400-£800 ). However, if the turbo has suffered internal bearing failure or oil starvation, a full Toyota 1ND-TV engine replacement or comprehensive rebuild is often the most reliable long-term solution.

items.title: Injector Seal Leaks ("Black Death")
items.whatHappens: The copper washer seals at the base of the fuel injectors can degrade over time, allowing combustion gases to escape into the valve cover. This creates a thick, black, tar-like sludge around the injectors, which can eventually corrode the cylinder head or cause misfires.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacing the injector seals is a relatively inexpensive and straightforward repair (£200-£400 ). If caught early, it rarely warrants a full unit replacement, but ignoring it can lead to catastrophic head damage.

items.title: DPF and EGR Clogging (Urban Use)
items.whatHappens: As a small-displacement diesel, the 1ND-TV is highly sensitive to short, urban journeys. The Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) cannot complete active regeneration, leading to soot accumulation, restricted exhaust flow, and subsequent strain on the turbocharger and EGR valve.
items.repairVsReplace: A professional DPF clean or forced regeneration can resolve early-stage clogging. If the blockage has caused severe backpressure and collateral turbo damage, Toyota 1ND-TV engine replacement is often the most cost-effective fix.

failures.goodYearsLine: The 1ND-TV is generally considered a robust and durable engine block. Most reported failures are ancillary (turbo, injectors, EGR) rather than catastrophic internal failures, making it a strong candidate for reconditioning rather than scrapping .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the 1ND-TV
variants.intro: The 1ND-TV engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, typically located on a machined pad near the junction of the engine and gearbox, or on a manufacturer sticker affixed to the timing belt cover. It is also clearly listed in your vehicle's V5C registration document under the "Engine Capacity" or "Engine Code" section, and can be definitively verified via a VIN decode. The 1ND-TV is sometimes confused with the larger 1AD-FTV or 2AD-FTV 2.0-litre D-4D engines, or the older 1CD-FTV. While they share Toyota's D-4D common-rail architecture, the 1ND-TV is a distinct 1.4-litre unit with specific ECU mapping, turbo sizing, and mounting points. Fitting a non-1ND-TV replacement without comprehensive ECU and loom modifications will result in poor performance, incorrect boost levels, and potential limp mode.

relatives.description: - the larger 2.0L D-4D variant; owners of larger Auris or Avensis models should look here, as it shares the common-rail architecture but has distinct head gasket failure patterns not present in the 1.4L unit.
- the 2.2L D-4D variant, sharing the AD-series common-rail architecture with higher output and specific head gasket vulnerabilities, making it a different replacement proposition entirely.
- the same physical 1.4-litre block was supplied to Mazda and Ford for the Mazda2 and Fiesta, though the Toyota-specific ECU mapping and turbo calibration mean they are not a straight swap.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement 1ND-TV - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Toyota 1ND-TV engine can be a budget-friendly choice for older Yaris or Auris hosts, provided the seller can supply documented evidence of regular servicing and no history of turbo or injector issues. The primary risk is inheriting a clogged DPF or a failing turbocharger that will require immediate post-purchase attention.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: This is the recommended route for most 1ND-TV owners. A proper reconditioned unit will have the turbocharger, injector seals, and EGR valve rigorously tested or replaced, and the DPF professionally cleaned or renewed. This eliminates the most common failure points of the 1.4 D-4D and restores the engine to near-factory reliability.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high-mileage examples where the core block is sound, but ancillary components (such as the high-pressure fuel pump or turbo) show significant wear. Ensure the rebuild specification explicitly addresses the Toyota D-4D emissions hardware to prevent recurring issues.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Booking through our network ensures your 1ND-TV is installed by specialists familiar with Toyota diesel systems, backed by a minimum 12-month warranty and nationwide delivery.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: With typical host vehicles (Yaris XP90/XP130, Auris E150) valued between £1,500 and £6,000 , a reconditioned 1ND-TV replacement can approach 40-60% of the vehicle's value on older examples. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing.

items.question: How much does a Toyota 1ND-TV engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A Toyota 1ND-TV engine replacement typically costs between £1,500 and £2,800 for a reconditioned supply-only unit . Fitted costs add approximately £390-£520 for independent specialist labour. Used units are available from £600, though they carry higher risk regarding turbo and injector health.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the 1ND-TV 1.4 D-4D?
items.answer: The most documented failure patterns for the 1ND-TV are turbocharger actuator wear and injector seal leaks, typically occurring between 80,000 and 150,000 miles . Turbo actuator wear leads to power loss, excessive black smoke, and limp mode. Injector seal leaks ("Black Death") cause thick carbon buildup around the injectors if not addressed promptly.

items.question: Which Toyota models use the 1ND-TV engine?
items.answer: The 1ND-TV engine was fitted to the Toyota Yaris (XP90/XP130) and Toyota Auris (E150) between 2004 and 2015. It was primarily marketed as the fuel-efficient entry-level diesel alternative for urban and commuter drivers. It is also found in some early Mazda2 and Ford Fiesta models, though the Toyota calibration is specific.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned 1ND-TV engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned 1ND-TV engine is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the known wear patterns of the turbocharger and injector seals. A proper recon will address or replace the turbo actuator, injector seals, and EGR valve. Used units often inherit clogged DPFs or failing turbos, leading to immediate post-purchase repair bills.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the 1ND-TV engine?
items.answer: You can confirm your vehicle has the 1ND-TV engine by checking the V5C registration document or the manufacturer sticker on the timing belt cover. The code is also stamped on a machined pad near the engine and gearbox junction. Do not confuse it with the larger 1AD-FTV or 2AD-FTV, as fitting the wrong revision can cause ECU and mounting incompatibility.
